cases.title: R (on the application of Bano) v London Borough of Waltham Forest
cases.anon: R (on the application of the Appellant) v A London Borough Council (local housing authority)
issues: On the proper construction of section 193(7AA) of the Housing Act 1996, does the main housing duty cease automatically when the applicant accepts or refuses a compliant private rented sector offer, without the authority having to make and notify a further decision that the offer was accepted or refused?
Was the Offer Letter itself a decision of the authority that was capable of being the subject of a request for review under section 202(1) of the Housing Act 1996?

Did the authority's communications after the Offer Letter, to the extent they merely affirmed that the main housing duty had ended, constitute decisions giving rise to a fresh right to request a review under section 202(1)?
cases.summary: The Court held that on its plain words section 193(7AA) ends the main housing duty by operation of law when the applicant accepts or refuses a compliant offer; no further authority decision or notification is required. This was supported by the contrast with section 193(5)(c), by the amendment history of section 193(7), and by the absurdity of the contrary reading. Section 202 still works, because the Offer Letter is itself the notified, reviewable decision that the duty will end on acceptance or refusal, with the 21 days running from the letter and time extendable under section 202(3). The Court rejected the absurdity and procedural fairness arguments, noting a letter not received would mean no acceptance or refusal and the duty would continue. It disagreed with the Court of Appeal that purely confirmatory later letters are reviewable, since that would circumvent the 21-day limit and the discretion to extend time; the error did not affect the outcome. The Appellant had a suitable alternative remedy by way of section 202 review, which precluded judicial review.
cases.evidence: Para 111: "Mrs Bano had a suitable alternative remedy by way of review under section 202 which precludes her claim for judicial review. We would dismiss the appeal." See also para 97: "We would dismiss this ground of appeal." and para 102 (grounds 1 and 2 dispose of the appeal). Lord Reed, Lord Sales and Lord Hamblen agree with Lord Stephens and Lady Rose (para 6 header).

claude-haiku.t: The first issue is one of statutory construction. Section 193(7AA) provides that the authority "shall also cease to be subject to the duty" if the applicant, having been informed in writing of the matters in s 193(7AB), accepts or refuses a private rented sector offer. The words are self-executing. Parliament used the phrase "notify" in s 193(5)(c) and did not use it here, and the legislative history of s 193(7) confirms the omission was deliberate. The appellant's reading would insert a further decision and notification requirement not found in the text. That reading would also leave the duty continuing indefinitely in cases where the authority simply fails to write. Automatic cessation therefore applies. The unfairness concerns the appellant raises (short deadlines, non-attendance treated as refusal, letters going astray) are addressed by the review and discretionary extension provided in s 202(3), and by the statutory requirement that the offer letter be in writing and warn of the consequences. On the second issue, the Offer Letter is itself a decision by the authority that the offer will discharge the duty on acceptance or refusal. It is notified in writing, and it is the decision on suitability that s 202(1)(g) and (1A) make reviewable. The 21-day period in s 202(3) runs from its notification. It is therefore capable of review. On the third issue, later letters that merely affirm that the duty has ended are not fresh decisions giving a new right of review. Allowing them would circumvent the 21-day limit. Judicial review is therefore unavailable because the statutory review and appeal under ss 202 and 204 provide the suitable remedy, which the appellant did not timely use. The appeal is dismissed.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues. The questions are whether section 193(7AA) operates automatically, whether the Offer Letter was a reviewable decision, and whether the later letters were fresh decisions.

Law. Section 193(7AA) provides that the authority "shall also cease to be subject to the duty" if the applicant, having been informed in writing of the section 193(7AB) matters, accepts or refuses a private rented sector offer. Other cessation provisions, such as section 193(5)(c), expressly require notification or satisfaction. Parliament's omission of such words in (7AA) is deliberate. The legislative history, in which post-refusal satisfaction and notification requirements were removed, confirms this. The word "possible" in (7AB) is explained by the chance of a successful suitability challenge.

Application. Issue 1: the duty ends by operation of law on acceptance or refusal of a compliant offer. The Appellant's reading would add words. It would also leave the duty alive indefinitely, even for a tenant who had moved in, if the authority failed to notify. Concerns about unfair deadlines or lost letters can be met on a section 202 review, and by extensions of time.

Issue 2: the written Offer Letter, which the statute requires, is the authority's notified decision that the duty will end on acceptance or refusal and that the offer is suitable. The 21-day period under section 202(3) runs from it. Section 202 therefore works coherently, and a review followed by a section 204 appeal was the suitable alternative remedy to judicial review.

Issue 3: later letters merely affirmed that the duty had ended and were not fresh decisions. Treating them as such would circumvent the 21-day limit. The authority's concession that a timely review would have succeeded does not change the analysis. The remedy was available and was not used.

Conclusion. The appeal is dismissed.

claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** The first issue is whether the main housing duty ends automatically on acceptance or refusal of a private rented sector offer. The second is whether the Offer Letter was a decision that could be reviewed under section 202. The third is whether the later letters that only affirmed the duty had ended gave a fresh right of review.

**Law.** Section 193(3) says the duty continues until it ends under one of the listed provisions. Section 193(7AA) says the authority "shall also cease to be subject to the duty" if the applicant, having been told in writing of the section 193(7AB) matters, accepts or refuses the offer. The subsection says nothing about the authority deciding, being satisfied or notifying. Section 193(5)(c), by contrast, expressly requires notification, so Parliament knew how to require it. The legislative history points the same way, because post-refusal decision requirements were removed. The duty therefore ends by operation of law. The word "possible" in section 193(7AB) reflects the chance that a challenge to suitability succeeds.

**Application.** The Offer Letter had to be in writing and was notified to the applicant. It was the authority's decision that the offer was suitable and that the duty would end on acceptance or refusal. It was reviewable under section 202(1)(b) and (g), and time ran from its notification, subject to the authority's power to extend time under section 202(3). Section 202 therefore works coherently without a separate discharge decision. The practical concerns raised can be met by extensions of time, by review, and by public-law control in truly exceptional cases. The Appellant's construction is also unworkable, since the duty could survive indefinitely through administrative oversight. Anufrijeva is met because the decision was communicated. The later letters only confirmed what had already happened by operation of law. They were not fresh decisions, and treating them as such would get round the 21-day limit. A section 202 review was the suitable alternative remedy.

**Conclusion.** The appeal is dismissed.

cases.title: R v Sheikh and others
issues: Where an act causing serious physical harm to a vulnerable adult was utterly different in its mechanism from antecedent violence inflicted on the victim, is that necessarily fatal to the requirement of foresight in section 5(1)(d)(iii) of the 2004 Act?
Did the Court of Appeal err in holding that the submission of no case to answer on the section 5 counts should have succeeded?
Was the trial judge's summing up on section 5(1)(d)(iii) defective such that the convictions are unsafe?
cases.summary: The Supreme Court held that section 5(1)(d)(iii) focuses on the circumstances in which the act occurred, not on the act or its kind, and that 'circumstances of the kind' do not need to be identical or closely correspond to those giving rise to awareness of risk; this broad reading accords with the statute's purpose of addressing harm inflicted in private by unidentifiable household members. The provision is not otiose, since it protects a defendant where the act occurred in circumstances of a kind not foreseen or foreseeable. The nature of the act or mechanism of harm may be one relevant circumstance but is not determinative. The Court of Appeal erred by treating the 'utterly different' mechanism of injury as dispositive to the exclusion of wider circumstances (hostility, the known earlier injury, neglect, isolation) and by substituting its view for the jury's; the trial judge was right to reject the no-case submission. The summing up, which followed the statutory wording, was correct and needed no paraphrase, and the Court of Appeal's other criticisms were unfounded.
cases.evidence: Para 67: "I would set aside the order of the Court of Appeal allowing the appeals against conviction of the respondents on counts 1 to 3 and 5 and reinstate those convictions." Para 66: "Lambert J was correct to dismiss the submissions of no case to answer on counts 1 to 5; ... Lambert J did not misdirect the jury in relation to counts 1 to 5." Para 68: "I would answer the question in the negative."

claude-haiku.t: The appeal turns on whether the foresight requirement in s 5(1)(d)(iii) of the Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004 is satisfied where the harm was caused by an act utterly different in mechanism from known antecedent violence. The Crown's broad reading treats any deliberate harmful act in a known abusive household as falling within "circumstances of the kind" foreseen. The Defendants' narrow reading would make the sub-paragraph add nothing to limbs (i) and (ii). Neither extreme is correct. "Circumstances of the kind that D foresaw" calls for a fact-sensitive comparison of the circumstances in which the harm occurred with those D foresaw or ought to have foreseen. Those circumstances include the victim's known injury, hostility, isolation and neglect, as well as the mechanism. Uzma Khan confirms the circumstances need not be identical. Mechanism is relevant to that comparison but is not dispositive. The Court of Appeal erred in treating the difference between a caustic agent and glimepiride as "utterly different" and therefore fatal. The sacral lesion, known to everyone in the household and plausibly inflicted deliberately, was a circumstance a jury could find was of a kind the Defendants ought to have foreseen. The submission of no case to answer should therefore not have been upheld on the sacral-injury basis, although the brain-injury basis is weaker and required separate evaluation. On the summing up, a direction in the bare statutory words was not itself defective, but the jury needed guidance on how to compare circumstances. The Court should restore the convictions only so far as the sacral-injury basis is concerned, and order a retrial or otherwise leave the remaining convictions quashed. Sanctions for the Crown's permission route are not an obstacle, since s 33(2) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968 provides the jurisdiction.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues. The questions are (1) whether a difference in mechanism between the antecedent violence and the harmful act is necessarily fatal to section 5(1)(d)(iii); (2) whether the Court of Appeal erred on no case to answer; and (3) whether the summing up was defective.

Law. Section 5 turns on a non-perpetrating defendant's awareness of the risk, a failure to protect, and, under (d)(iii), the act occurring "in circumstances of the kind that D foresaw or ought to have foreseen". Sub-paragraph (iii) is a real limiting requirement. If it were satisfied almost automatically once (i) and (ii) were proved, it would have no function. It protects a defendant from liability for any unlawful act whatever within the household. The circumstances need not be identical, as Khan recognised. They must still be of a kind that the defendant foresaw or ought to have foreseen. The question is one of ordinary meaning and is for the jury, but only if properly directed.

Application. Issue 1: a difference in mechanism, here a caustic agent against a drug, is relevant but not necessarily fatal. The statute speaks of the circumstances of the act, not the method of harm. The Court of Appeal was wrong to treat "utterly different" as dispositive. Circumstances such as the victim's isolation, hostility towards her, neglect and a known earlier injury could amount to circumstances of the same kind. The Crown's "save in wholly exceptional circumstances" gloss is nevertheless too broad. It would remove the safeguard Parliament enacted.

Issue 2: on that approach a jury could properly find the condition met for at least some defendants. The no-case ruling was therefore not clearly wrong on the broad ground the Court of Appeal gave.

Issue 3: the judge adopted the Crown's broad reading and gave the jury the bare statutory words. Without guidance that (iii) requires a real connection between what the defendant foresaw and the circumstances of the act, the jury could not properly decide the issue. The convictions are unsafe on that ground. The Court of Appeal's conclusion should stand, with the reasoning corrected.

Conclusion. The Crown's appeal is dismissed. Any question of retrial is for the Crown.

claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** The first issue is whether section 5(1)(d)(iii) of the Domestic Violence, Crime and Victims Act 2004 fails as a matter of law where the act that caused the harm worked in a completely different way from the earlier violence. The second is whether the submission of no case to answer should have succeeded. The third is whether the summing up was defective.

**Law.** Section 5 was designed for one problem. Serious harm is inflicted in private, and every member of the household can avoid conviction because nobody can prove who did it. Paragraph (d)(iii) is a real and separate safeguard. Proof that D was aware of a risk under (d)(i) and failed to protect V under (d)(ii) does not automatically satisfy it. However, the provision asks about the "circumstances" in which the act occurred, not the act itself or its mechanism. Those circumstances only need to be "of the kind" D foresaw or ought to have foreseen. They need not be identical (R v Khan [2009] EWCA Crim 2). The circumstances include the relationship, the hostility shown to V, her isolation and dependency, and the deliberate harm already done to her. Whether the circumstances are "of the kind" is an ordinary-language question of fact for the jury (Brutus v Cozens).

**Application.** I reject the Crown's near-presumption that any deliberate harm will qualify, because it would empty (d)(iii) of content. Even so, the Court of Appeal treated the difference between a caustic agent and glimepiride as decisive. That was a mistake. V was a dependent and isolated adult. She had been left with an untreated, obviously agonising injury that had been deliberately inflicted. A jury could properly conclude that each Defendant ought to have foreseen further deliberate harm to her in that setting, whatever method was used. The submission of no case was rightly rejected. The judge directed the jury in the words of the statute, which are ordinary words. The jury did not need a gloss, and the direction did not make the convictions unsafe.

**Conclusion.** The appeal is allowed and the convictions are restored.

cases.title: Augustine v Data Cars Limited
issues: Does the right in regulation 5(1) of the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 apply only where part-time status is the sole ground of the less favourable treatment, such that it is not enough that part-time status is an effective cause of it?
cases.summary: The Supreme Court held that regulation 5(2)(a) is satisfied where part-time status is an effective cause of the less favourable treatment, and that it need not be the sole cause. The phrase "on the ground that" had a well-established meaning in discrimination law by 2000, covering significant or effective causes and not only sole ones. The Court found it unnecessary to decide what "solely because" means in clause 4.1, because no conforming construction was required. Section 19 of the 1999 Act and clause 6.1 allowed the Regulations to give wider protection than the Directive, and the Secretary of State chose established domestic wording instead of "solely". The word "only" in regulation 5(2) qualifies both conditions and does not set a causation test, and the singular "ground" refers to the single protected status. A sole-cause test would produce unreasonable outcomes, and other causes are relevant to objective justification and compensation. McMenemy was wrongly decided on this point and the Court of Appeal's contrary approach was in error.
cases.evidence: Para 87: "For these reasons (which are essentially the same as those given by the Court of Appeal majority), I would allow the appeal. The 2000 Regulations prohibit less favourable treatment of part-time workers where their part-time status is an effective cause of the impugned treatment. It need not be the sole cause." Lady Simler gave the judgment, with whom Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Hamblen, Lord Leggatt and Lord Richards agreed (header, para 10).

claude-haiku.t: The question is whether reg 5(1) and (2) of the Part-Time Workers Regulations 2000 apply only where part-time status is the sole ground of the less favourable treatment. The Regulations were made to implement Directive 97/81/EC, and clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement prohibits less favourable treatment "solely because" a worker works part time. The domestic words "on the ground that" must be read consistently with that purpose, so far as the language permits, and the CJEU has consistently applied a sole-cause test (Wippel). The appellant's argument that "on the ground that" in English discrimination law means an effective or substantial cause is an argument about the Equality Act and the Employment Rights Act regimes, which are not the instrument in question. Section 19 of the Employment Relations Act 1999 is an enabling power to implement the Directive, not a signal that Parliament intended a wider test than the Directive requires. The Regulations are carefully limited to direct discrimination with an actual comparator and objective justification, and the singular "ground" contrasted with the wording of regs 6 and 7 supports a single-cause test. Consistency with the Directive also means the sole-ground test is not inconsistent with the Regulations' scheme. On the facts, the uniform fee was charged to generate revenue as is the industry norm, so part-time status was not the sole ground. Both courts below were bound by McMenemy, and the Court of Appeal was right to apply it. The appeal is dismissed.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issue. The question is whether regulation 5(2)(a) of the 2000 Regulations, which requires treatment "on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker", demands that part-time status be the sole ground, or only an effective cause.

Law. "On the ground that" is established language in discrimination law. Nagarajan and O'Neill establish that the protected characteristic need only be an effective or substantial cause, not the sole cause. The Regulations do not use "solely". Section 19 of the Employment Relations Act 1999 empowers wide protection. Clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement uses "solely because", but the Regulations must be read consistently with the Directive so far as possible. The CJEU has not decided that "solely" excludes a case with several causes. Wippel states the principle only in the language of the clause. MK v Lufthansa and Lalfi treated other reasons as going to objective justification. A sole-cause reading would let employers escape liability by adding a second criterion, which would defeat the purpose of the Directive and Regulations. That purpose is to eliminate discrimination against part-time workers.

Application. Properly construed, the Directive's "solely because" asks whether the less favourable treatment is attributable to part-time status. It does not ask whether a second, independent cause also exists. Other causes are relevant to objective justification. The Operator did not seek to justify the fee. The fixed weekly fee operated so as to treat part-time drivers less favourably per hour, and part-time status was at least an effective cause of that disadvantage. The commercial reason for the fee, revenue generation, is a justification matter and does not negate the causal link. McMenemy was wrongly decided on this point and should not be followed.

Conclusion. The appeal is allowed. The sole-ground test is rejected and the matter is remitted, or the claim upheld, on the basis that effective cause suffices.

claude-opus.t:
**Issue.** Does regulation 5 of the Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 apply only where part-time status is the sole ground of the less favourable treatment?

**Law.** Regulation 5(2)(a) uses the phrase "on the ground that". That phrase has a settled meaning in domestic anti-discrimination law: the protected status must be an effective cause, though not necessarily the only or main cause (Nagarajan; O'Neill; Fecitt). The Regulations were made under the wide power in section 19 of the Employment Relations Act 1999. Clause 6.1 of the Framework Agreement expressly permits more favourable provision. The drafter did not copy the Directive's words "solely because" and chose familiar domestic language instead. The word "only" in regulation 5(2) introduces the conditions on which the right depends. It does not describe the causal test. In any event, the CJEU's references to the "sole ground" have not been used to defeat claims where part-time status was a cause alongside others. In cases such as Lufthansa CityLine and Lalfi, the court treated other reasons as matters of objective justification. A sole-cause test produces arbitrary results, because an employer could escape liability by adding a second criterion (Sharma). It would also undermine the purpose of removing discrimination against part-time workers. The structure of the Regulations, with justification and just and equitable compensation, deals with mixed motives. McMenemy was wrongly decided on this point.

**Application.** A flat fee charged to every driver means that, on the pro rata principle, part-timers pay more per hour. Part-time status is therefore an effective cause of the less favourable treatment. The Operator's revenue-raising purpose and possible software limits go to justification, which it did not attempt to make out.

**Conclusion.** The appeal is allowed. The sole-ground test is rejected, and the claim succeeds subject to remedy.

cases.title: Avon Freeholds Limited v Cresta Court E RTM Company Limited
cases.anon: The Freeholder v The RTM Company
issues: Does a failure by an RTM company to give a notice of invitation to participate to a qualifying tenant, in breach of sections 78(1) and 79(2) of the 2002 Act, invalidate the claim notice or otherwise prevent the RTM company from being entitled to acquire the right to manage, so that a landlord can rely on it in a counter-notice under section 84(2)(b)?

Is the statement in A1 Properties (Sunderland) Ltd v Tudor Studios RTM Co Ltd [2024] UKSC 27 at para 69, that section 79(2) means no valid claim notice can be given if NIPs have not been given, part of the ratio decidendi of that case, or otherwise a statement this Court should follow here?
cases.summary: The Supreme Court held that breach of sections 78(1) and 79(2) does not invalidate the claim notice and cannot found a counter-notice objection to entitlement. Applying the Soneji principle, section 79(2) is a timing rule for claim notices and not an express sanction for breach of section 78(1). The scheme divides into substantive entitlement conditions, which alone can ground a dispute about entitlement under section 84, and a procedural code. The NIP rules are procedural and protect qualifying tenants, who have no right to object. The Freeholder was not protected by them and suffered no prejudice. The proper remedy is a discretionary order under section 107. The statement in A1 Properties at para 69 was not part of the ratio and should not be followed, so the Upper Tribunal's decision was restored.
cases.evidence: Para 81: "For those reasons I would allow this appeal, and restore the decision of the Upper Tribunal." Para 65 states the conclusion: "the statutory scheme in the 2002 Act does not impose invalidity of the claim notice as the sanction for breach of either or both of sections 78(1) and 79(2)." Lord Briggs gave the judgment, with which Lord Reed, Lord Stephens, Lady Rose and Lord Snowden agreed.

claude-haiku.t:
The question is whether an RTM claim notice given in breach of ss.78(1) and 79(2) of the 2002 Act is invalid, so that a landlord may rely on that defect in a s.84(2)(b) counter-notice. The agreed facts are that the omitted tenant was eligible, joined the company and supported the claim, and that all substantive eligibility conditions were met on the relevant date.

Section 79(2) provides that the claim notice "may not be given" unless every person entitled to a NIP has had one at least 14 days before. That is mandatory and prohibitory language, and it sits in the entitlement conditions of the claim rather than in mere form. Section 84(2)(b) allows a counter-notice alleging non-entitlement "by reason of a specified provision" of the Chapter, and s.79 is such a provision. The appellant's Soneji analysis is not needed where the statute addresses the consequence. The express invalidity provisions in ss.78(7) and 81(1) concern only inaccuracies in particulars, and they do not show that Parliament meant to exclude invalidity for a failure to comply with s.79(2). The purpose of the NIP requirement is that all qualifying tenants should be invited to participate before the claim is made. The later joining of the tenant cannot cure the defect, because the statute fixes the position at the date of the claim notice.

The appellant's alternative of treating the notice as valid for fixing the relevant date but invalid for success is unattractive. A claim notice is either valid or it is not, and a notice cannot be partly effective for one statutory purpose.

On issue 2, the statement in A1 Properties at para 69 is a considered reading of the very provision now in issue, and it was necessary to the reasoning in that case. Settlers Court is consistent with it. The Court should follow it, and the Court of Appeal was right to do so.

Conclusion: the claim notice was invalid, the counter-notice succeeds, and the appeal is dismissed.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues: (1) whether failure to give a NIP to a qualifying tenant invalidates the claim notice or defeats entitlement so that a counter-notice under s.84(2)(b) can rely on it; (2) the status of para 69 of A1 Properties.

Law: Where a statute prohibits an act but prescribes no consequence, the court asks what Parliament intended, looking to purpose and the interests protected (R v Soneji), not whether the provision is mandatory or directory. Chapter 1 of Part 2 separates entitlement conditions (ss.72-75, 79(3)-(5)), which a counter-notice under s.84(2)(b) may challenge, from the procedural code. Parliament expressly provided for invalidity in some places (ss.78(7), 81(1)). Section 107 gives a remedy for non-compliance.

Application: The NIP requirement exists to protect qualifying tenants by giving them an opportunity to join and to be told of the claim. It does not protect the landlord, who has no say in whether the tenants participate. The landlord suffers no prejudice. The tenant concerned joined days later, supported the claim and has never complained. Treating the claim notice as a nullity would defeat the legislative aim of a scheme designed to reduce landlord obstruction, and would give a landlord a technical windfall. Section 79(2) is a prohibition without a stated consequence, so it falls within Soneji. The intended consequence is not nullity of the notice as against a landlord. The remedy lies in s.107 and in tenants' own rights. The statement in A1 Properties at para 69 was obiter, because the case concerned s.79(6) and this question was reserved. It was made without argument and need not be followed. Section 79(2) is not an entitlement condition that s.84(2)(b) can invoke, and breach does not prevent entitlement.

Conclusion: appeal allowed. The claim notice was valid and the RTM Company was entitled to acquire the right to manage.

claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** The first question is whether a failure to give a notice of invitation to participate (NIP), in breach of ss.78(1) and 79(2), makes the claim notice invalid, or otherwise stops the RTM company being entitled to acquire the right to manage, so that the landlord can rely on it in a counter-notice under s.84(2)(b). The second is the status of para 69 of A1 Properties.

**Law.** Where a statute does not state what follows from non-compliance, the court asks what Parliament intended, looking at the purpose of the requirement and the scheme as a whole (R v Soneji). Section 79(2) says a claim notice "may not be given". It does not say that a notice given in breach is a nullity. Where Parliament wanted to deal with validity, it did so expressly (ss.78(7) and 81(1)). In Settlers Court and A1 Properties this Court stressed that the scheme is meant to be simple and to keep the landlord's chances to obstruct the claim to a minimum. A1 Properties was about s.79(6). Para 69 dealt with a point that was not before the Court and was reserved, so it is obiter.

**Application.** The NIP requirements protect qualifying tenants, who cannot object or serve a counter-notice. They do not protect the landlord. A counter-notice under s.84(2)(b) must allege that the company was not entitled to acquire the right to manage. That goes to the substantive conditions in ss.72 to 77 and s.79(3) to (5), and all of them were met on the relevant date. The tenant who was left out joined the company within days and supported the claim, so nobody was prejudiced. If an omitted tenant does complain, s.107 lets the court order the failure to be made good. Treating the notice as void would bring the uncertainty and obstruction that the scheme is designed to avoid. The landlord's alternative, that the notice is valid for some purposes but not others, has no basis in the Act.

**Conclusion.** The failure to give a NIP does not invalidate the claim notice and gives the landlord no ground for a counter-notice. Para 69 of A1 Properties is not binding and should not be followed. Appeal allowed, and the FtT's determination restored.

cases.title: Forthwell Limited v Pontegadea UK Limited
issues: Does Scots law permit a contracting party to recover, on behalf of a third party and as a matter of general legal policy, the third party's loss caused by a breach of contract, in circumstances falling outside the narrow Albazero ground and the broader St Martins ground (the Panatown/Lord Clyde solution)?
On the pleaded facts, is the Tenant entitled to recover the Subsidiary's loss of profits from the Landlord as transferred loss?
cases.summary: The Supreme Court held that Lord Clyde's Panatown solution was not endorsed by any other member of the House of Lords, does not represent the law of England and Wales, and is contrary to Swynson, where the exception rests on the contracting parties' intention rather than a rule of law. Lord Drummond Young's adoption of it in McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton was therefore based on an error. The proposed exception is also too wide, because it allows recovery where the third party was not within the parties' contemplation at contracting, and too indefinite, because the limits of the 'material interest' test are vague. The Court saw no cogent case for the exception, noting the third party rights legislation and that legal black holes are rare. The outcome is not unjust, since the Tenant and the Subsidiary chose their corporate structure and the licence appears to breach the lease. The First Division was correct. The Court also observed that the narrow Albazero exception is part of Scots law, and left open whether the broader ground is part of English or Scots law.
cases.evidence: Para 44: "For these reasons the First Division was correct to allow the reclaiming motion. I would dismiss the appeal." Para 1: Lord Doherty gives the judgment, with which Lord Reed, Lord Stephens, Lady Simler and Lord Hodge agree. Para 3: counsel agreed that "if it is unsuccessful the appeal should be dismissed."

claude-haiku.t:
The question is whether Scots law should adopt Lord Clyde's solution in Panatown, under which a contracting party may recover a third party's loss, and whether on the pleaded facts the Subsidiary's lost profits are recoverable as transferred loss. The Tenant accepts that neither Albazero nor St Martins applies.

Scots law recognises third-party rights, but the contract remedy for breach is ordinarily confined to the claimant's own loss, which is the performance interest. The House of Lords in Panatown did not produce a majority for Lord Clyde's approach, and Swynson treats transferred loss as an exception of narrow scope, justified by the parties' intention or by legal necessity. A general Scots rule that a contracting party recovers any third party's loss would extend the exception well beyond those grounds, and it would also make a contracting party account to third parties for sums it had recovered. The black-hole argument does not justify that extension, because the Subsidiary has its own contractual position and the law can address gaps through other means. I would not adopt the general solution.

Even if a narrower solution were available, the pleaded case fails on its own facts. The licence provides that the Tenant is not liable to the Subsidiary for deficiencies, so the Tenant has no liability to account and no material interest in the Subsidiary's profits. The lease prohibits sub-letting and sharing possession, so the Subsidiary's occupation is itself unauthorised. No common contractual intention to benefit the Subsidiary is shown. The Landlord could not have contemplated that the Tenant would recover the Subsidiary's losses on this footing. The majority in the First Division was right that the transferred loss claims should be dismissed.

Conclusion: the appeal fails, and the transferred loss claims are dismissed.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues: (1) whether Scots law recognises Lord Clyde's Panatown general transferred-loss solution; (2) whether the Tenant can recover the Subsidiary's loss on these facts.

Law: The general rule is that a pursuer recovers only its own loss. Transferred loss is a limited exception (Albazero; St Martins; Swynson), grounded in the contracting parties' common intention that a third party would benefit and in legal necessity, so that no legal black hole arises. Lord Clyde's wider solution in Panatown was not adopted by the other Law Lords and was obiter. Lord Drummond Young's endorsement in McLaren Murdoch was likewise obiter, and Scots law has now legislated for third party rights in the 2017 Act.

Application: The Tenant disclaims the Albazero and St Martins grounds and relies solely on the Clyde solution. A free-standing policy-based power to recover a stranger's loss, subject only to a vague "material interest", would be uncertain, would risk double recovery and would undermine the rule that damages compensate the claimant's own loss. It is also unnecessary here. The Tenant can sue for its own loss, including specific implement and damages for its own interest in the repair. The lease prohibits sub-letting and sharing possession. The licence expressly excludes any duty on the Tenant to repair or account to the Subsidiary, and the Landlord was not aware of it. There was no common intention to benefit the Subsidiary and no gap in remedies caused by necessity. The claim does not satisfy even the recognised exceptions.

Conclusion: appeal dismissed. Scots law does not recognise the Clyde solution as a general principle, and the transferred loss claims are irrelevant.

claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** The first question is whether Scots law recognises Lord Clyde's general-policy route to transferred loss, outside the narrow Albazero ground and the broader St Martins ground. The second is whether, on the pleadings, the Tenant can recover the Subsidiary's lost profits.

**Law.** The basic rule in Scots law, as in English law, is that a pursuer recovers damages only for its own loss. Transferred loss is a narrow exception. It rests on what the contracting parties must be taken to have intended, and it is justified only where the law truly needs it, so that a loss within the parties' contemplation does not go uncompensated (Albazero, Linden Gardens, Panatown, Swynson). In Panatown, Lord Clyde's wider approach was not adopted by the majority, and his remarks were obiter. Lord Drummond Young's adoption of it in McLaren Murdoch & Hamilton was also obiter. A rule that lets any contracting party with a "material interest" sue for the losses of members of its group is not a principled limit. It would cut across the corporate veil and across the 2017 Act's careful regime for third-party rights. Scots law's history of recognising third-party rights does not require a general policy-based transfer of loss.

**Application.** The Subsidiary's lost profits are consequential losses of a separate legal person. There is no common intention of the original contracting parties to benefit it. The Landlord did not know of the licence, and the lease forbids sharing possession. Under the licence the Tenant owes the Subsidiary nothing, so there is no real reason to make it account for what it recovers. Nor is there a legal black hole: the Tenant can sue for its own performance interest, and the Subsidiary's loss arises from the group's own arrangements. Even if the Lord Clyde approach were available, these pleadings would not meet it.

**Conclusion.** Both issues are answered no. Appeal dismissed.

cases.title: R (on the application of Quaye) v Secretary of State for Justice
cases.anon: R (Appellant) v Secretary of State for Justice
issues: Does the exclusion, by section 27A of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997, of any right to a minimum term review for persons aged 18 or over when sentenced to detention during His Majesty's pleasure give rise to a risk of arbitrary detention contrary to article 5 ECHR?

Is the difference in treatment between persons sentenced to detention during His Majesty's pleasure when under 18 and those sentenced when aged 18 or over, as regards the right to apply for a minimum term review under section 27A, without objective and reasonable justification, so as to be incompatible with article 14 read with article 5 ECHR?

Does removal of the opportunity to apply for a minimum term review for those aged 18 or over when sentenced impose a heavier penalty than the one applicable when the offence was committed, contrary to article 7(1) ECHR?
cases.summary: The Court held that section 82A of the 2000 Act had fundamentally changed DHMP, so continuing review of the minimum term was no longer an inherent feature of the sentence. Sections 27A and 27B put minimum term reviews on an entirely statutory footing. Article 5 was not breached, because the minimum term was lawfully fixed by the court, had a sufficient causal link to the conviction, and Strasbourg case law does not require such a term to be reviewable. On article 14 read with article 5, the Court applied a wide margin of appreciation and its own fresh proportionality assessment. The legitimate aim of reducing distress to victims' families was served by a bright line at age 18 at sentence, in primary legislation that Parliament had considered carefully. Retrospectivity carried little weight, because the Revised Policy had already removed the opportunity and there was no right to an executive review. Article 7 was not engaged, because review concerned early release and the execution of the sentence rather than the penalty itself, which remains an indefinite sentence with a court-fixed minimum term.
cases.evidence: Para 145: "For all these reasons, sections 27A and 27B of the 1997 Act are compatible with articles 5, 7 and 14 read with article 5 of the ECHR. ... The difference in treatment provided for by section 27A is objectively justified. Accordingly, we would dismiss the appeal." (Lord Stephens and Lady Simler, with whom Lord Sales, Lord Briggs and Lord Hamblen agree.)

claude-haiku.t: The appellant's three grounds are considered in turn. On article 5(1)(a), the detention is lawful because it results from a court-imposed minimum term and a sentence of detention during His Majesty's pleasure. Strasbourg authority (Saadi, James) leaves the length of a sentence causally linked to conviction to national authorities absent bad faith. Continuing review for DHMP detainees was a feature of executive practice and clemency (Venables, Smith), not a requirement of article 5. Release remains available through the Parole Board, so the absence of a minimum-term review does not render detention arbitrary. On article 14 read with article 5, the difference between those sentenced under 18 and those sentenced at 18 or over is a difference in age at sentence, and age is not a suspect ground. The margin of appreciation is wide for primary legislation on penal policy. Parliament drew a bright line at 18 at sentence, rejected a higher cut-off, and the policy removing review for this group had already applied since 2021 without challenge. The legitimate aim of avoiding distress to victims' families is a real and proportionate aim, and the line is not manifestly without reasonable foundation. On article 7, a minimum-term review concerns early release and the execution of the sentence, not the penalty imposed. The penalty was fixed by the court when the offence was committed and remains the same. Del Rio Prada and Kupinskyy are distinguishable, and Kafkaris and Hogben support that conclusion. The appeal is dismissed, and the Court of Appeal's order quashing the declarations is upheld.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues. The questions are whether excluding those aged 18 or over at sentence from the minimum term review under section 27A engages article 5 as arbitrary detention; whether it is unjustified discrimination under article 14 with article 5; and whether it imposes a heavier penalty contrary to article 7.

Law. Under article 5(1)(a), detention after conviction by a competent court is lawful. Its length, absent bad faith or a similar vice, is for national authorities (Saadi; James). Nothing in Strasbourg law requires every indeterminate sentence imposed on an offender who was a child at the time of the offence to be reviewable. Article 14 requires that a difference in treatment between analogous groups be objectively and reasonably justified. A wide margin applies to primary legislation on penal and social policy. Age is not a suspect ground. Article 7 concerns the scope of the penalty, not its execution or release arrangements (Kafkaris; Hogben; Morgan).

Application. Issue 1: the minimum term was fixed by a judge under section 82A after proper process and was open to appeal, and the sentence remains subject to Parole Board release. Continuing executive review is no longer inherent in DHMP since the judge took over setting the term. The earlier review policy was clemency. The absence of a review mechanism does not make the detention arbitrary.

Issue 2: even if the two groups are analogous, Parliament's choice of a line at 18 at sentence is justified. It reflects the law's general age lines. It serves the legitimate aim of sparing victims' families repeated distress, and Parliament considered and rejected a higher age. The sentencing guidelines for children were fully applied at the sentencing stage. The revised 2021 policy, which is unchallenged, had already removed eligibility for this group, so nothing was taken from the Appellant by the statute. The line is not manifestly without reasonable foundation.

Issue 3: the review concerns early reduction of the term, which is a matter of execution. The penalty imposed remains a court-set minimum term with the possibility of release, so Del Río Prada and Kupinskyy are distinguishable.

Conclusion. The appeal is dismissed and the declarations of incompatibility remain quashed.

claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** There are three challenges to section 27A of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997, under article 5, article 14 read with article 5, and article 7 of the ECHR.

**Article 5.** The Appellant's detention follows a conviction by a competent court, and there is a clear causal link between them. The minimum term was fixed judicially under section 82A after a proper process and could be appealed. Under Saadi and James, the length of the punitive term is a matter for national authorities, absent bad faith or similar arbitrariness. Since the minimum term passed to the courts, continuing review of the punitive part has not been an inherent feature of detention during His Majesty's pleasure. The earlier executive policy was an act of clemency and not a legal entitlement. Release after the minimum term remains in the hands of the Parole Board. No Strasbourg authority requires a minimum term imposed on a child to be reviewable. There is no real risk of arbitrary detention.

**Article 14 with article 5.** I assume the claim falls within the ambit of article 5 and that the two groups are analogous. Age at sentence is not a suspect ground. This is primary legislation on penal and social policy, Parliament debated the cut-off, and a wide margin applies. The aim of reducing repeated distress to victims' families is legitimate. A bright line at 18, the general age of adulthood, is a rational and proportionate way to pursue it. The Appellant had already lost access to review under the 2021 policy, which he does not challenge. The difference in treatment is objectively justified.

**Article 7.** Article 7 is concerned with the penalty imposed, not with arrangements for its execution or early release (Kafkaris; Hogben; Morgan). The penalty remains an indeterminate sentence with a court-fixed minimum term and the possibility of release. Taking away a chance of discretionary reduction does not redefine or extend the scope of that penalty. Del Río Prada and Kupinskyy are therefore distinguishable.

**Conclusion.** The appeal is dismissed.

cases.title: ScottishPower (SCPL) Limited and others v Commissioners for His Majesty's Revenue and Customs
cases.anon: The Energy Group Companies v HMRC
issues: Is expenditure on penalties imposed by a regulator non-deductible in computing trading profits because, on the construction of s.54(1)(a) CTA 2009, it is not incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade, rather than because of a separate judge-made adjustment under s.46(1) CTA 2009?
Are the Redress Payments paid under the settlement agreements, together with a nominal £1 penalty, to be treated like penalties and so non-deductible under s.54(1)(a) CTA 2009?
Is the sum of about £554,013 paid to customers affected by mis-selling, which the First-tier Tribunal found to be compensatory, deductible even if the other Redress Payments are not?
cases.summary: The Supreme Court held that penalties are non-deductible because, by their nature (punishment of the taxpayer and deterrence), expenditure on them is not incurred for the purposes of the trade within s.54(1)(a); Lord Hoffmann's reference in McKnight to legislative policy was not a separate judge-made rule under s.46(1), so the Court of Appeal misread it. Looking at substance rather than form, the Redress Payments were not truly voluntary: the Supplier would otherwise have faced penalties of similar size, the decision notices linked the payments to the penalty that would have been imposed, and they were made in place of a penalty. They were therefore sufficiently akin to penalties to fall outside s.54(1)(a), regardless of the £1 penalty, the payees, or the accounting treatment. Herald and Weekly Times was irrelevant, and the £554,013 compensatory element was part of the same package and not to be treated differently. HMRC's appeal was allowed and the Upper Tribunal's decision restored.
cases.evidence: Para 100: "We would therefore allow HMRC's appeal and restore the decision of the Upper Tribunal." Para 94: "We have no doubt that the Redress Payments are sufficiently akin to penalties for it to be clear ... that they were not expenditure incurred for the purposes of ScottishPower's trade within the meaning of section 54(1)(a)."

claude-haiku.t:
The question is whether the regulator's penalties and the settlement Redress Payments are deductible under CTA 2009 ss.46 and 54(1)(a).

On issue 1, the non-deductibility of penalties is a judge-made policy rule, from Strong v Woodifield, Warnes, von Glehn and McKnight v Sheppard, which operates as an adjustment under s.46(1) and applies even where the purpose test in s.54(1)(a) is met. It is not a matter of construing "wholly and exclusively" alone. The answer to issue 1 is therefore no.

On issue 2, the Redress Payments are not all penalties in form. Only a nominal £1 was imposed, and most of the payments went to customers and charities. However, the FtT found as a fact that, absent settlement, a penalty of the same order would probably have been imposed, and that the payments were negotiated as one package in place of that penalty. The policy against deducting penalties would be undermined if a taxpayer could secure deduction for the same economic burden by calling a penalty "redress" under the regulator's auspices. The non-compensatory element is therefore to be treated as a penalty and is non-deductible. The answer to issue 2 is yes, to that extent.

On issue 3, the FtT found that about £554,013 was compensatory payment to mis-sold customers, akin to damages for loss caused by the breach. Such a sum is not a penalty in substance and is deductible. The answer to issue 3 is yes.

The Court of Appeal erred in treating the whole package as deductible. The Upper Tribunal erred in denying deduction for the compensatory sum. The appeal is allowed in part: the non-compensatory Redress Payments are non-deductible, and the compensatory sum is deductible. Confidence in this outcome is low, because the case turns on how the Court views the characterisation of the package.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues: (1) the basis of non-deductibility of penalties; (2) whether the Redress Payments plus a £1 penalty are to be treated as penalties; (3) whether the £554,013 compensatory element is deductible.

Law: Section 54(1)(a) CTA 2009 asks whether expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade. The authorities (Strong v Woodifield, Warnes, von Glehn, McKnight) show that penalties for breach of regulatory requirements are not deductible. The rationale is public policy, or the dilution of the statutory scheme (Lord Hoffmann in McKnight), and not merely the purpose test. It operates as a judge-made adjustment "required or authorised by law" under s.46(1). Because it is a policy-based exception, it should be narrowly confined and not extended to sums that are not penalties. Form is not wholly decisive, but the court looks at substance.

Application: The Supplier chose to settle and was not compelled. Only a nominal £1 penalty was imposed. The settlement discounts and the redress payments went to customers and charities, not the Consolidated Fund. These were negotiated remedial payments, not penalties imposed by the regulator. The finding that a large penalty would probably have followed if contested is speculation about a counterfactual that did not occur. Treating them as penalties would extend the adjustment beyond its policy and is a matter for Parliament, which has separate consumer redress provisions. The purpose test is satisfied on the facts found (avoiding the risks and costs of contest and protecting the trade). Compensation to mis-sold customers is in any event closer to damages and is deductible.

Conclusion: appeal dismissed. The Redress Payments are deductible.

claude-opus.rec: HMRC v ScottishPower (SPUK) Ltd and others
claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** There are three questions:
1. Is the rule against deducting penalties a matter of construing s.54(1)(a), or a separate adjustment under s.46(1)?
2. Are the Redress Payments to be treated like penalties?
3. Does the compensatory sum of about £554,013 stand apart?

**Law.** From Strong v Woodifield, Warnes and von Glehn through to McKnight, penalties have been treated as non-deductible because a fine for breaking the law is not, by its nature, spent for the purposes of the trade. It is imposed on the trader as a wrongdoer in order to punish. Lord Hoffmann's reference in McKnight to diluting the penal scheme explains why the rule exists. It does not create a separate adjustment outside s.54(1)(a). The question is one of construing the statute, and the court looks at the substance and character of the payment.

**Application.** The FtT found that the settlements were made in place of penalties of a similar size that would otherwise probably have been imposed. The payments were negotiated with the regulator as one package, within its penalty policy, which credits redress in setting a penalty. They were made in respect of admitted breaches and in exchange for a nominal £1 penalty. The fact that the money went to customers and charities rather than to the Consolidated Fund does not change its character as a penal sanction accepted in place of a fine. Otherwise taxpayers who settle would be treated differently from taxpayers who contest, for no good reason. The mis-selling sum was part of the same global settlement, accepted as part of the regulatory sanction. It is not a free-standing payment of damages, and Herald and Weekly Times does not apply. The UT was right not to break the package apart.

**Conclusion.**
1. Yes: the rule is one of construing s.54(1)(a).
2. Yes: the Redress Payments are to be treated like penalties.
3. No: the compensatory sum is not deductible either.

Appeal allowed, and the UT's decision restored.

cases.title: The Kingdom of Spain and another v The London Steam-Ship Owners' Mutual Insurance Association Limited (No 2)
cases.anon: The Insurer v Two Sovereign States
issues: Where a third party enforces a right derived from a contract containing an arbitration clause and so becomes bound to arbitrate, and an injunction and damages in lieu are unavailable because the third party is a State, can the tribunal or court nevertheless award monetary compensation to the other contracting party for loss caused by the breach of that obligation?

Did the Court of Appeal, on an appeal under s.69 of the Arbitration Act 1996, exceed the statutory limits of such an appeal by relying on matters (causation and international comity) that the tribunals had not been asked to determine and on which permission had not been granted?
cases.summary: The Court held that an obligation to arbitrate arising under the conditional benefit principle is a contractual obligation owed at common law, not an equitable one. The third party is treated as a party to the contract for this purpose. Equitable compensation is therefore not the correct remedy. The correct remedy is common law damages for breach of contract. The Court rejected the Court of Appeal's four reasons. The principle's 'defensive' character does not exclude monetary relief. The unavailability of an injunction and s.50 damages against a State does not remove common law damages, which are not coercive. The Spanish courts' decisions did not displace the States' breach as an effective cause of the loss. Causation and comity were outside the scope of a s.69 appeal. Damages for past breaches, including conditional orders to pay if future losses arise, can be awarded at common law. Only pure quia timet relief for future breaches fails. There was no issue estoppel and no need to remit, so the awards were confirmed, with a recital added and the word 'equitable' deleted.
cases.evidence: Para 155: "For these reasons, we would allow the appeal. ... Subject to these variations, the awards should be confirmed." Para 154: "We conclude that there is no warrant for remitting the awards to the arbitrators ..." Para 99: "an obligation to arbitrate arising by operation of the conditional benefit principle is a contractual obligation owed at common law and not an equitable obligation. ... equitable compensation is not an available remedy."

claude-haiku.t:
The question is whether, where a State is bound to arbitrate by the conditional benefit principle and injunctions and s.50 damages are unavailable under s.13(2)(a) of the State Immunity Act 1978, a tribunal may still award monetary compensation for breach of that obligation. The second question is whether the Court of Appeal exceeded the limits of a s.69 appeal.

The conditional benefit principle requires a party that enforces a contractual right to accept the contract's arbitration clause. The obligation is in substance a negative obligation not to sue elsewhere, and its natural remedies are injunction, declaration and, where available, damages in lieu under s.50. Equitable compensation developed under Target Holdings and AIB v Redler for breach of equitable duties and is not an independent route. Allowing a monetary indemnity for future losses, in respect of foreign enforcement, would achieve indirectly what s.13(2)(a) forbids directly, and would sit uneasily with the immunity scheme. The Appellant's losses were also caused in substance by the Spanish courts' rejection of the pay-to-be-paid defence and by its own decision not to appear, rather than by the breach of the obligation to arbitrate. The Court of Appeal was right to set aside the monetary awards on that basis.

On issue 2, a s.69 appeal is confined to a question of law arising from the award, and the court's powers are limited to the questions the tribunal decided. The Court of Appeal's reliance on comity was tied to the question whether the power exists at all, which was an issue the tribunal had to address, so I would not hold that it exceeded its jurisdiction. The point is not decisive in any event. There is no need to remit, because the claim was always put on the footing of equitable compensation and the Appellant has not shown that a different legal basis would survive.

Conclusion: the appeal is dismissed.

claude-sonnet.t:
Issues: (1) whether monetary compensation is available for breach of the obligation to arbitrate where an injunction and s.50 damages are barred by the State Immunity Act; (2) whether the Court of Appeal exceeded the limits of a s.69 appeal.

Law: Under the conditional benefit principle, a third party who enforces a contractual right must accept its burdens, including the arbitration clause. The obligation is a primary obligation, and breach of it sounds in a monetary remedy. Equitable compensation is available for breach of an equitable obligation. Section 13(2)(a) of the 1978 Act prohibits only injunctions (and specific performance) and does not bar monetary relief. Section 50 is merely an additional power and does not restrict other remedies. The question under s.69 is a question of law arising from the award. Sharp v Viterra confines the appellate court to the question of law and to the facts found.

Application: The States' obligation not to sue other than in arbitration is a real obligation. Breach by suing in Spain causes loss, and a monetary remedy is less intrusive than an injunction and does not circumvent the immunity statute. The principle has produced positive money obligations. Nothing in the 1978 Act or the nature of the principle denies compensation. The Court of Appeal's conclusion that there was no power to award compensation was wrong. The Court of Appeal also relied on causation and comity, which were not raised before the tribunals or covered by the permission, and so exceeded the limits of s.69. On the other hand, the characterisation as equitable compensation is doubtful, and causation, remoteness and the future indemnities may require re-examination by the tribunals, so the awards cannot simply be confirmed.

Conclusion: appeal allowed in part. Monetary relief is available in principle, but the awards are remitted to the tribunals to consider the legal basis, causation and scope.

claude-opus.rec: London Steam-Ship Owners' Mutual Insurance Association Ltd v Kingdom of Spain and French State (The Prestige)
claude-opus.t:
**Issues.** The first question is whether monetary compensation can be awarded against a non-party State that is bound to arbitrate under the conditional benefit principle, when an injunction and s.50 damages are not available. The second is whether the Court of Appeal went beyond the limits of a s.69 appeal.

**Law.** A third party who enforces a contractual right takes it subject to the arbitration clause. It is bound to pursue the right only by arbitration (The Jay Bola, Aspen). That is a real obligation, and breaking it can cause loss that is recoverable. The cases recognise money awards where the obligation is broken. Section 13(2)(a) of the State Immunity Act bars only relief "by way of injunction". Section 50 of the Senior Courts Act only adds remedies; it does not limit others. Section 9(1) removes immunity from proceedings relating to the arbitration. On a s.69 appeal, the court is confined to the questions of law that arise from the award and on which permission was given (Sharp v Viterra).

**Application.** The States chose to enforce a contractual right, so they are bound to arbitrate. It would make no sense if the immunity from coercive injunctive relief left the insurer with no remedy for loss caused by their breach. A compensatory award is less intrusive than an injunction and does not get round s.13(2)(a). The award is properly seen as compensation for breach of a primary obligation, whatever label is attached to it. Whether the losses were caused by the breach was a matter of fact for the tribunals. They found that the insurer acted reasonably in not appearing in Spain. The Court of Appeal's reliance on causation and comity went outside the questions of law properly before it. The future-loss indemnities are conditional orders for losses that flow from breaches already committed.

**Conclusion.** Issue 1, yes. Issue 2, yes. Appeal allowed, and the monetary parts of the awards restored.
